newsitem.title: UK: Dlr drifts in Europe as France takes centre stage.
newsitem.headline: Dlr drifts in Europe as France takes centre stage.

text.p: The dollar drifted against the mark and yen in Europe's afternoon, its sentiment soft, as the market turned its attention firmly to an expected snap French election and its implications for European monetary union.

The dollar was dragged down early in the day by the overall strength of the mark, which gained on its European counterparts as speculation of a French election sparked new doubts about Europe's single currency. The possibility of France's power passing into the hands of a Socialist-led alliance made markets fear that France, a core candidate for EMU, may have difficulty balancing pro-EMU policies with efforts for economic growth.

The spotlight would likely remain on the European situation for now and not the U.S. or Japan, analysts said, although they added that this would change as the market braced for the meeting of G7 finance ministers this weekend.
"The focus will be very much on whether there will be more weakness in the European currencies against the mark," said Chris Turner, currency strategist at BZW in London.

"It (the dollar) could be pretty soft this week... There's the G7 coming up and there's also very little data coming out, and it's hard to see where the dollar is going to get a boost from," Turner said.
The dollar was at 1.7032/39 marks at 1523 GMT against 1.7126/36 in late Europe on Friday, after barely managing to stop short of falling below the key 1.70-marks level.
It was at 125.53/63 yen against 125.88/93 late on Friday after moving in a 0.6-yen range throughout an uninspired European session.

"There's been surprisingly little movement in dollar/yen, considering there's been so much focus on it recently. In Europe it definitely seems to have taken second place behind the French franc," said a trader at a U.S. bank here.

The franc fell to its lowest against the mark in more than a month, and other European currencies were dragged down with it. French President Jacques Chirac met his prime minister and parliamentary leaders this morning and was due to broadcast to the nation at 1800 GMT.

Analysts, however, said the shock of a snap French election, expected to be held in late May or early June, was unlikely to linger in the currency market for very long -- especially as Chirac's ruling coalition was expected to win again, albeit with a smaller majority.
"Ultimately, an early election could be good for France; if Chirac wins they can press ahead with fiscal consolidation," said BZW's Turner.

Meanwhile, six leading German economic institutes forecast the nation's public sector deficit would be between 3.0 and 3.2 percent of GDP this year, but there was little reaction to this. Rather, the market was awaiting the European Commission's 1997/98 economic forecasts for EU member states, due Wednesday.
There was also little impact from data showing that Germany's M3 money supply, a key indicator, grew by 8.3 percent in March compared with 9.1 percent the previous month.
The M3 data was in line with expectations but above the Bundesbank's target range of 3.5 to 6.5 percent.

The British pound was mixed, softening against the mark in line with the rest of the market and strengthening on the dollar. Sterling was at 2.7819/29 marks and $1.6341/51 against late Friday's 2.7959/64 and $1.6312/22.
